reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
clinicalPearls: A highly vascular CNS WHO grade 1 tumour arising most often in the cerebellum, but also the spinal cord, brainstem and retina.
The classic imaging pattern is a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule, and MRI frequently shows serpentine flow voids from feeding and draining vessels.
Around a quarter of cases occur in von Hippel-Lindau disease, where tumours are often multiple and present at a younger age.
A VHL diagnosis mandates screening for retinal haemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and pancreatic and endolymphatic lesions.
Stromal cells produce erythropoietin, so a minority of patients present with secondary polycythaemia that resolves after resection.
Histology shows lipid-laden vacuolated stromal cells within a dense capillary network, and the stromal cells are typically inhibin-alpha positive.
Preoperative angiography and embolisation can reduce intraoperative bleeding from these vascular tumours.
Metastatic clear cell renal carcinoma is the key mimic and must be excluded, particularly in VHL patients.
reference.pathophysiology: Haemangioblastoma is a benign, highly vascular neoplasm composed of neoplastic stromal cells and an abundant capillary network. The stromal cell is the tumour cell, and in von Hippel-Lindau disease it carries biallelic inactivation of the VHL tumour suppressor; sporadic tumours also show somatic VHL loss. Loss of functional VHL protein prevents degradation of hypoxia-inducible factors, so HIF-alpha accumulates and constitutively drives transcription of vascular endothelial growth factor and erythropoietin. This produces the exuberant capillary proliferation that characterises the tumour and, through erythropoietin, can cause secondary erythrocytosis. The vacuolated, lipid-rich cytoplasm of the stromal cells reflects this dysregulated hypoxia-response programme.
additionalDifferentials: metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma
cerebral or cerebellar metastasis of other origin
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and whole spine
catheter angiography to define vascular supply and enable embolisation
abdominal imaging for renal, adrenal and pancreatic lesions
plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
full blood count for secondary polycythaemia and erythropoietin level
dilated retinal examination for retinal haemangioblastoma
redFlags: obstructive hydrocephalus from a posterior fossa lesion
progressive myelopathy from a spinal cord tumour
coexisting phaeochromocytoma causing labile blood pressure
reference.prognosis: Complete resection of a solitary tumour is usually curative with an excellent outlook, but patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease develop multiple and recurrent lesions over time and require lifelong surveillance.
pitfalls: mistaking metastatic renal cell carcinoma for haemangioblastoma, especially in VHL
failing to screen for von Hippel-Lindau disease and its associated tumours
operating without appreciating the vascularity and risk of catastrophic bleeding
overlooking an occult phaeochromocytoma before anaesthesia
attributing polycythaemia to a primary haematological cause rather than the tumour
